block.label: supported
block.says: Casa Batlló is on Passeig de Gràcia, in a row known as the Illa de la Discòrdia, the Block of Discord, named for its strikingly different buildings by noted Modernista architects.
quote: Casa Batlló is located on the Passeig de Gràcia in the Eixample district and forms part of a row of houses known as the Illa de la Discòrdia (or Mansana de la Discòrdia, the "Block of Discord"), so named because it features four striking, and strikingly different, buildings by noted Modernista architects of Barcelona.

rivalry.label: supported
rivalry.says: In 1898 the chocolatier Antoni Amatller hired Josep Puig i Cadafalch, who added a Flemish stepped gable; Francesca Morera then hired Lluís Domènech i Montaner in 1902; and Josep Batlló, owner of the house next to Casa Amatller, hired Gaudí in 1904 to put the others to shame.
quote: A fierce rivalry started in 1898, when the chocolatier Antoni Amatller hired architect Josep Puig i Cadafalch to reform a building at Passeig de Gràcia 41, which Puig did by adding a Flemish stepped gable and lavish neo‑gothic ornament. This provoked Francesca Morera just a few doors away to hire architect Lluís Domènech i Montaner in 1902 to renovate a building she had inherited, in this case in a florid Catalan art nouveau style. Textile industrialist Josep Batlló, owner of the house adjacent to Casa Amatller, then hired Gaudí in 1904 to put the others to shame.

finest.label: supported
finest.says: A historian writes that the city's wealthy industrialists "fought with each other to build the finest house on the street."
quote: "united to combat the anarchist‑led working class, but fought with each other to build the finest house on the street."

amatller.label: supported
amatller.says: Casa Amatller, by Puig i Cadafalch, was the home of Antoni Amatller and then his daughter until 1960, so its 1900 interior is largely preserved; it is now a house museum.
quote: After his death in 1910, it remained the home of Amatller's daughter until her death in 1960. The continuous ownership by the Amatller family meant that the house's interior of 1900 has remained largely preserved intact to the present day. It now serves as a historic house museum

renovation.label: supported
renovation.says: Batlló first wanted to tear the old building down; Gaudí convinced him a renovation was enough, and it was finished in 1906.
quote: In 1904, Josep Batlló hired Gaudí to design his home; at first his plans were to tear down the building and construct a completely new house. Gaudí convinced Josep that a renovation was sufficient
The building was finished and refurbished in 1906.

award.label: supported
award.says: In 1906 the city council shortlisted the house for best building of the year, but the award went to another architect.
quote: That same year (1906), the Barcelona City Council selected the house as a candidate for that year's best building award. (Despite Gaudí's trailblazing design, the award was given to another architect.)

bones.label: supported
bones.says: Locally it is called Casa dels ossos, the House of Bones, for its skeletal look.
quote: The local name for the building is Casa dels ossos (House of Bones), as its biomorphic aesthetic has a skeletal quality.

facade-parts.label: supported
facade-parts.says: The lower floors are Montjuïc sandstone with undulating lines; the main floor has fine columns that look like the bones of a limb, and its gaping openings earned it the nickname house of yawns.
quote: The lower ground floor with the main floor and two first-floor galleries are contained in a structure of Montjuïc sandstone with undulating lines.
are six fine columns that seem to simulate the bones of a limb
for which the Casa Batlló has been nicknamed the "house of yawns."

masks.label: supported
masks.says: The balconies have iron railings in the shape of masks.
quote: with iron railings in the shape of masks

lake.label: supported
lake.says: The central façade evokes a lake with water lilies, covered with colored glass and 330 rounds of colored pottery, the discs designed by Gaudí and Jujol.
quote: The central part of the façade evokes the surface of a lake with water lilies
It is a great undulating surface covered with plaster fragments of colored glass discs combined with 330 rounds of polychrome pottery. The discs were designed by Gaudí and Jujol

trencadis.label: supported
trencadis.says: The broken-tile mosaic shards on the façade were collected from the dumpsters of other building sites, according to one architecture critic.
quote: "The trencadís mosaics made from broken tile shards" on "the façade of Casa Batlló were collected from the dumpsters of other construction sites," notes Gomez-Moriana

dragon-roof.label: supported
dragon-roof.says: The arched roof recalls a dragon's spine with ceramic tiles for scales, shading from green on the right to blue and violet in the center to red and pink on the left; a small triangular window toward the right is the eye.
quote: The roof's arched profile recalls the spine of a dragon with ceramic tiles for scales; a small triangular window towards the right of the structure simulates the eye.
with the color grading from green on the right side, where the head begins, to deep blue and violet in the center, to red and pink on the left side of the building

lance.label: disputed
lance.says: A common theory says the rounded tower with a cross, left of centre, is the lance of Saint George, patron saint of Catalonia, plunged into the dragon's back.
quote: A common theory about the building is that the rounded feature to the left of centre, terminating at the top in a turret and cross, represents the lance of Saint George (patron saint of Catalonia, Gaudí's home), which has been plunged into the back of the dragon.

george-legend.label: legend
george-legend.says: In the legend, Saint George defeats a dragon that demanded tribute from villagers and saves a princess chosen as its next offering.
quote: Saint George and the Dragon is a legend in which Saint George—a soldier venerated in Christianity and among the Druze—defeats a dragon. The story goes that the dragon originally extorted tribute from villagers.
One day, the princess herself was selected as the next offering.

house-dragon.label: supported
house-dragon.says: Casa Batlló is known as the House of the Dragon because of its Saint George symbolism.
quote: Casa Batlló, which is considered among Gaudí's finest works, is known as "House of the Dragon" due to its Georgian symbolism.

holy-family.label: supported
holy-family.says: The tower carries ceramic monograms of Jesus, Mary and Joseph in gold; the bulb arrived broken, and Gaudí liked it and had the pieces fixed in place.
quote: monograms of Jesus (JHS), Maria (M with the ducal crown) and Joseph (JHP) made of ceramic pieces that stand out in gold against the green background
The bulb was broken when it was delivered. Gaudí liked the aesthetic of the broken masonry and asked that the pieces be stuck to the main structure

no-straight.label: supported
no-straight.says: Gaudí observed: "There are no straight lines or sharp corners in nature. Therefore, buildings must have no straight lines or sharp corners."
quote: "There are no straight lines or sharp corners in nature," he famously observed. "Therefore, buildings must have no straight lines or sharp corners."

atrium.label: supported
atrium.says: The central light well is tiled in shades of blue, deeper at the top and paler toward the bottom, so light spreads evenly to every floor; Gaudí wanted the bottom to feel like the bottom of the sea.
quote: The wall of the atrium is done in different shades of blue
The blue tiles allow an equal distribution of light to all the floors.
Gaudí wanted to make the bottom of the well feel like the bottom of the sea.
The blue tiles are more intensely colored at the top and more opaque toward the bottom of the atrium.

noble.label: supported
noble.says: The main floor, the Batlló family's home, has skylights like tortoise shells and a mushroom-shaped fireplace in a nook for courting couples.
quote: it is accessed through a private entrance hall with skylights resembling tortoise shells
a secluded spot for courting couples, notable for its mushroom-shaped fireplace

loft.label: supported
loft.says: The white loft, once laundry and storage, has sixty catenary arches like an animal's ribcage.
quote: It was formerly a service area for the tenants of the different apartments in the building which contained laundry rooms and storage areas.
It contains a series of sixty catenary arches that creates a space which represents the ribcage of an animal.

unesco.label: verified
unesco.says: UNESCO lists Casa Batlló, a pre-existing building remodelled by Gaudí, among the Works of Antoni Gaudí.
quote: the Casa Batlló, a pre-existing building remodelled by Gaudí

parts.name: The Block of Discord
parts.stand: Stand on the far side of Passeig de Gràcia, across from the colorful house with the scaly roof, so you can see its neighbors too.

paras.t: Look at this stretch of the avenue. Locals call it the Block of Discord, because of these strikingly different buildings, side by side, each by a famous architect.

It was a rich men's contest. In 1898 the chocolate maker Antoni Amatller had his house redone by Josep Puig i Cadafalch, with that stepped Flemish gable. In 1902 Francesca Morera, a few doors along, answered with Lluís Domènech i Montaner. Then in 1904 Josep Batlló, Amatller's next-door neighbor, hired Gaudí, to put the others to shame.
One historian puts it perfectly. The city's industrialists "fought with each other to build the finest house on the street."
Casa Amatller, the one with the stepped gable, stayed in the family until 1960, so its rooms from 1900 are still largely intact. It's a house museum now.

parts.name: The façade
parts.stand: Stay across the street, facing Casa Batlló.

paras.t: And here's Gaudí's answer: Casa Batlló. Batlló wanted to knock the old house down. Gaudí talked him into transforming it instead, and it was done by 1906.
Locals call it the House of Bones. Look at the lower floors. Those thin columns look like the bones of a limb, and the balcony railings above are shaped like masks.

The middle of the façade is meant to suggest a lake with water lilies. It sparkles with colored glass and 330 round pottery pieces, designed by Gaudí with Josep Maria Jujol. According to one critic, the broken tile was gathered from the dumpsters of other building sites.
Gaudí famously said, "There are no straight lines or sharp corners in nature. Therefore, buildings must have no straight lines or sharp corners." See if you can find one here.
In 1906 the city shortlisted it for building of the year. It lost, to another architect.

Now the roof. That arched ridge is the back of a dragon, with ceramic tiles for scales. Green on the right, where the head begins, then blue and violet, then pink and red on the left. The small triangular window toward the right is its eye.

Why a dragon? There's an old legend of Saint George, a soldier saint who defeats a dragon, a dragon that had demanded the princess herself as its next offering. George is the patron saint of Catalonia, and this is known as the House of the Dragon.
That rounded tower with the cross, left of center? A common theory says it's George's lance, plunged into the dragon's back. Nobody knows for sure if Gaudí meant it that way.
On that tower, look for the gold letters for Jesus, Mary and Joseph. The bulb on top arrived broken. Gaudí liked it that way and had the pieces fixed in place.

parts.name: Inside
parts.stand: If you go in, stop on the main floor landing where you can see down the blue light well.

paras.t: This blue shaft is the light well. The tiles are deeper blue at the top and paler lower down, so the light spreads evenly to every floor. Gaudí wanted the bottom to feel like the bottom of the sea.
On this floor lived the Batlló family. Look up for skylights shaped like tortoise shells, and find the mushroom-shaped fireplace, tucked into a little nook for courting couples.
Up in the white loft, the old laundry, sixty arches curve overhead like the ribs of an animal. And then you step out onto the dragon's back.
Today UNESCO lists Casa Batlló as World Heritage. Not bad for an old house that was nearly torn down.

parts.name: Closing
parts.stand: Back out on the avenue, take one last look up.

paras.t: It started as a contest between neighbors, to show off. Gaudí took that bit of vanity and turned an ordinary old house into a dragon, a lake and a legend, right in the middle of the street.
